Summer of Love
SUM-er uv LUV
proper noun (Boomer slang)
The name given to the summer of 1967, when as many as 100,000 young people converged on the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco, drawn by the Human Be-In (January), the Monterey Pop Festival (June), Scott McKenzie’s hit "San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair)" (May), and national press coverage of the hippie scene. Local organizers formed a "Council for the Summer of Love" in the spring; by October the Diggers staged a mock "Death of Hippie" funeral to mark its end.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Summer of Love is shorthand for 1967 in San Francisco: flowers in the hair, free concerts in the park, free food from the Diggers, LSD, communal crash pads, and the conviction that a new age of peace and freedom was dawning. Many grandparents remember it as the high-water mark of their youth. The Christian observation: it promised liberty and delivered bondage within a single season. Peter saw it nineteen centuries early: "While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption" (2Pe 2:19). By autumn the Haight was a slum of hard drugs, venereal disease, runaways, and predators; the Diggers held a funeral for the hippie in October. It was the law of the harvest working on schedule: "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Gal 6:7). And Jeremiah’s lament could have been written on a Haight Street wall that fall: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved" (Jer 8:20). Yet God did not abandon those children. Within three years, out of the same streets, the Jesus Movement was baptizing hippies in the Pacific by the thousands. The summer of love ended; the love of God did not. "The world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever" (1Jn 2:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

The name for 1967 in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury, when some 100,000 young people sought peace and free love — a promise of liberty that became bondage by autumn (2Pe 2:19), and a harvest that ended unsaved (Jer 8:20).

expand to see more

SUMMER OF LOVE, n. (proper; 1967) The summer of 1967, when tens of thousands of young people gathered in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury and elsewhere to celebrate the hippie counterculture of peace, free love, music, and drugs; used generally for the high point of 1960s idealism.

Webster (1828) — SUMMER, noun With us, the season of the year comprehended in the months June, July and August; during which time, the sun being north of the equator, shines more directly upon this part of the earth, which, together with the increased length of the days, renders this the hottest period of the year. In latitudes south of the equator, just the opposite takes place, or it is summer there when it is winter here. The entire year is also sometimes divided into summer and winter, the former signifying the warmer and the latter the colder part of the year.

Decode for families: the Summer of Love was followed by the fall of the Haight. Ask a grandparent what came after September.

Modern Corruption

The Summer of Love promised a new age of liberty and love and harvested addiction and exploitation by autumn; Scripture calls that the promise of liberty from servants of corruption (2Pe 2:19).

expand to see more

The romance of 1967 survives because it is remembered by the survivors. The runaways who never went home, the girls exploited in the crash pads, the young men burned out on speed and heroin by Christmas — they do not write the anniversary retrospectives. The Diggers themselves, who had fed the crowds all summer, carried a coffin down Haight Street in October 1967 marked "Hippie, Son of Media." The movement knew it had been sold something. Paul names the transaction: "he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption" (Gal 6:8).

The Christian telling of 1967 must not end there, because God’s story did not. The same young people who went west looking for love were met, a few years later, by the Jesus People — long-haired evangelists in the same streets with Bibles instead of tabs. Many of the Boomer generation’s pastors and missionaries came out of that wreckage. The summer ended; the harvest that saves did not. "He that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting" (Gal 6:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English sumor + love; spring 1967 "Council for the Summer of Love," San Francisco → the name for the whole 1967 hippie season.
